sections.section_title: Capnocytophaga canimorsus Infection After Dog Bite: Clinical Context and Early Disease Mechanisms
sections.description: This section introduces the zoonotic exposure, the microbiology of Capnocytophaga canimorsus, and the early sepsis syndrome that framed the initial presentation. It provides the background needed to understand why a dog bite can progress to fulminant infection and why the first working diagnosis was sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation rather than a primary thrombotic microangiopathy.
subtopics: Epidemiology and transmission of Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dogs and cats
Microbiological features: slow-growing, fastidious, encapsulated gram-negative rod
Spectrum of human disease: local infection, bacteraemia, septic shock, DIC, multiorgan failure, and rare TMA
Host defense against C. canimorsus and the role of complement in bacterial clearance
Why severe infection can occur in immunocompetent adults
Clinical relevance of delayed or missed post-bite antibiotic prophylaxis
Initial symptom evolution in this case: fever, malaise, hypoglycaemia, mottled extremities, and rapid deterioration
Pathophysiology of sepsis-related hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, coagulopathy, and organ dysfunction
Early differential triggered by the presentation: severe sepsis, DIC, necrotising soft tissue infection, acute haematologic disease, and HLH
Diagnostic limitations of blood culture in C. canimorsus and the role of modern molecular methods

sections.section_title: Initial Stabilisation and ICU Course: Managing Septic Shock, DIC, and Dialysis-Dependent Acute Kidney Injury
sections.description: This section follows the early inpatient course, emphasizing bedside recognition of sepsis-related multiorgan dysfunction, empiric treatment choices, supportive care, and the development of anuric acute kidney injury. It teaches how the initial syndrome was managed before the later emergence of thrombotic microangiopathy.
subtopics: Recognition of sepsis severity and interpretation of the initial laboratory pattern
Pancytopenia, coagulopathy, liver injury, metabolic acidosis, and AKI as manifestations of severe systemic infection
Reasoning behind empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic selection for dog-associated pathogens
Why piperacillin/tazobactam was appropriate pending organism identification
Excluding surgical emergencies such as necrotising fasciitis
ICU monitoring and organ support in evolving multiorgan dysfunction
Management of DIC: blood product support, fibrinogen replacement, and thrombocyte transfusion
Progression from preserved urine output to complete anuria
Indications for continuous renal replacement therapy in septic AKI with fluid overload and cardiomyopathy
Interpretation of distal cyanosis, ecchymoses, and preserved pulses in microthrombotic DIC
De-escalation of antibiotics once C. canimorsus bacteraemia was confirmed
Clinical clues suggesting recovery from sepsis and resolution of coagulopathy

sections.section_title: When the Course Changes: Recognising Superimposed Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: This section explains the pivotal diagnostic transition from resolving sepsis/DIC to a new syndrome of isolated haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and persistent kidney failure. It teaches learners how to detect thrombotic microangiopathy when it is initially masked by infection and coagulopathy.
subtopics: The significance of a sudden haemoglobin drop without bleeding in a recovering septic patient
Laboratory hallmarks of haemolysis: rising LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, and transfusion requirement
Persistent thrombocytopenia despite improvement in inflammation and coagulation parameters
Peripheral smear interpretation and the diagnostic importance of schistocytes
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia as a syndrome rather than a final diagnosis
Why DIC alone no longer fully explained the ongoing haematologic abnormalities
Direct antiglobulin test positivity: true autoimmune haemolysis versus false-positive results after penicillin exposure or transfusion
Why corticosteroids were started initially and why non-response mattered diagnostically
The relationship between TMA and acute kidney injury, including dialysis dependence and anuria
Clinical timing: why delayed haemolysis after initial sepsis improvement pointed toward an infection-triggered secondary process

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning in Adult TMA: Distinguishing DIC, TTP, STEC-HUS, and Complement-Mediated HUS
sections.description: This section presents a structured framework for evaluating thrombotic microangiopathy in adults, using the case to illustrate exclusion-based diagnosis. It integrates laboratory testing, biopsy interpretation, complement studies, and the strengths and limitations of each diagnostic tool.
subtopics: Definition of thrombotic microangiopathy and its core triad: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury
Comparing DIC and TMA: overlap, distinguishing features, and why both may coexist
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: clinical urgency, PLASMIC score, and ADAMTS13 activity threshold
Why ADAMTS13 activity of 43.5% effectively ruled out TTP in this patient
STEC-HUS in adults: typical history, stool PCR testing, and exclusion in this case
Complement-mediated HUS as a clinicopathological diagnosis of exclusion
Why normal C3 and C4 do not exclude complement-mediated HUS
Functional complement pathway assays and how treatment timing can confound interpretation
Kidney biopsy findings of TMA: fibrin thrombi, ischaemic glomeruli, acute tubular necrosis, and crescents
Role of immunofluorescence and electron microscopy in excluding immune complex or primary glomerular disease
Genetic and acquired causes of complement dysregulation: factor H, factor I, factor B, CD46, and anti-factor H antibodies
Concept of a trigger-plus-susceptibility model and the possibility of infection-triggered disease without identifiable mutation
Synthesising the evidence that supported the final diagnosis of C. canimorsus-triggered complement-mediated HUS

sections.section_title: Treatment Strategy, Outcome, and Clinical Lessons from Infection-Triggered Complement-Mediated HUS
sections.description: This section focuses on the therapeutic decisions made once complement-mediated HUS was suspected, including the use of plasma exchange as a bridge, initiation of eculizumab, infection-prevention measures, renal recovery, and long-term follow-up. It concludes with practical lessons for clinicians encountering TMA after sepsis.
subtopics: Immediate treatment priorities once TMA is suspected before the subtype is confirmed
Rationale for plasma exchange as bridging therapy while excluding TTP and arranging complement blockade
Mechanism of action of eculizumab and why C5 inhibition is standard therapy for complement-mediated HUS
Timing of eculizumab initiation in the setting of recent bacteraemia: balancing renal rescue against infectious risk
Vaccination requirements before terminal complement blockade: meningococcal serogroups and scheduling
Need for antimicrobial prophylaxis when vaccination cannot precede therapy by 2 weeks
Monitoring response: platelets, haemolysis markers, urine output, dialysis requirement, and kidney function
Interpreting the return of diuresis after plasma exchange and the sustained remission after eculizumab
Short-term and medium-term outcome in this patient: haematologic remission with partial renal recovery
Approach to maintenance therapy and reassessment for discontinuation when no pathogenic complement variant is found
Prognostic factors in complement-mediated HUS, especially baseline renal injury and delay to complement inhibition
Broader clinical lessons: consider rare infectious triggers of TMA, do not rely on normal C3/C4 to exclude CM-HUS, and revisit the diagnosis when the clinical trajectory changes
